title: Development of a Total Nutrient Index
text:
Dietary supplements are an important contributor to overall micronutrient (i.e. vitamins and minerals) exposures
for a large proportion of the population. We developed and validated a metric, the total nutrient index (TNI),
that captures multiple micronutrient exposures inclusive of supplements for use in research, clinical, and
monitoring settings. This current project will update the TNI to identify critical micronutrients and in what
combinations optimally benefit the health and nutrition of individuals across the life course, and relate the TNI
to risk factors, health outcomes, and mortality.

title: Hepatic Lymphatics and the Immune Response in Acute Liver Failure
text:
Liver recovery and regeneration after acute acetaminophen overdose dictate patient prognosis with
compromised recovery leading to acute liver failure. This proposal will investigate the role of hepatic lymphatics
in driving liver recovery after acute injury and determine how this influences the innate immune response
necessary for hepatocyte regeneration. This work will also test Wharton's Jelly mesenchymal stem cells as
novel therapy to facilitate reconstruction of the hepatic lymphatic network to hasten liver recovery.

title: Postdoctoral Training in Reproductive Mood Disorders
text:
Among females, reproductive mood disorders (peripubertal depression, postpartum depression, premenstrual
dysphoric disorder, and perimenopausal depression) are prevalent and associated with substantial morbidity
and mortality. Reproductive mood disorders are similar to other depressive disorders in symptom expression,
but they differ in their greater predictability of affective state change resulting from changing reproductive
hormone levels. Training the next generation of researchers in reproductive mood disorders will not only
increase our understanding of the causes of these debilitating disorders and aid in the identification of
therapeutic targets, but because reproductive mood disorders may serve as a model for studying affective
state change, our comprehension of the causes of mood disorders overall will also be advanced.

title: Genetics and Pathobiology of Disorders of Keratinization
text:
Genetic investigation in disorders of keratinization has identified many pathways important for
normal skin function. We propose to employ comprehensive genetic evaluation to identify
additional genetic causes of these disorders and to perform functional studies to gain insight
into mechanisms of skin disease. This work will benefit public health, as gaining insight into
genetic causes of these diseases will provide new information about how the skin maintains and
renews itself with implication for generation of new targeted therapies for these severe, rare skin
diseases.

title: Fetal cerebral arteries and prenatal alcohol exposure
text:
Fetal alcohol spectrum disorders (FASD) is a leading preventable cause of mental retardation in the
United States that develops in children whose mothers engaged into considerable alcohol consumption
during pregnancy. Currently, there is no readily available cure for FASD, and the goal of our research is
to establish the role of alcohol damage to fetal brain vessels in development of this pathology. If
successful, our research will introduce a much needed pathway for therapeutic intervention(s) against
FASD.

title: Impacts of hematopoietic stem cell aging on distant tissues
text:
This project details a study of how hematopoietic stem cell aging impacts the functions
of distant tissues and organismal aging. This study will have profound implications in
treating diseases of aging.

title: Project 2: Therapeutic Gene Editing for Friedreich's Ataxia
text: PROJECT 2 (FRDA) Friedreich's Ataxia (FRDA) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by progressive ataxia and damage to the nervous system, that is often associated with muscle weakness, spasticity, cardiomyopathy and diabetes mellitus. FRDA is caused by a deficiency in frataxin (FXN) protein levels that usually arises from a GAA-triplet repeat expansion in intron 1 of the FXN gene which results in transcriptional repression. The length of FXN GAA- repeats in the general population ranges from ~5-60, while FRDA patients may present with 66 to well over 1200 repeats, typically 600 to 900 repeats long. Long GAA-repeats undergo progressive instability in some somatic cell types that predominantly results in repeat expansion and consequently loss of FXN protein. The tissues that are affected in FRDA include the dorsal root ganglia (DRGs), the heart, and the pancreas. The onset of disease in patients is anticorrelated with the length of the shortest FXN allele, which typically presents at 10-15 years of age, though approximately 25% of patients have an atypical presentation with later disease onset. Although some symptoms can be ameliorated by physical therapy and surgery, no effective cure or treatment for the broader FRDA phenotype has yet been approved. The life expectancy for patients with FRDA is typically 40-50 years of age. In this follower project, we aim to improve FXN protein expression to enable rescue of disease progression in FRDA patients. Specifically, we aim to: (1) Optimize genome editing strategies to correct FRDA repeat expansion; (2) optimize genome editing strategies to correct FRDA repeat expansion in mice; and (3) perform pre-clincial IND enabling studies to assess safet and efficacy. We will work closely with the Gene Editing Core to develop the latest base editing and/or prime editing technologies in FRDA model systems. We will iterate with the Gene Editing Core to ensure that our genome editing tools maximize on-target editing efficiencies, minimize undesirable gene editing byproducts and off-target editing events, and maximize compatibility with in vivo delivery methods of potential therapeutic relevance.

title: Examination of Snord116 in Neuronal Ribosome Biology
text:
This project aims to characterize the molecular functions of Snord116 in ribosome biogenesis and protein
synthesis in neurons, addressing key gaps in understanding Prader-Willi syndrome. By identifying the immediate
consequences of Snord116 loss, we seek to uncover new therapeutic strategies to correct early events in
disease pathology. In the long term, this research will provide insights into how ribosomes are specifically
adapted to the neuronal environment, providing spatiotemporal translation control.

title: Next-generation nonstop gated CBCT for respiratory gating lung SBRT
text:
There is an urgent, unmet clinical need for more time- and dose-efficient gated cone-beam computed
tomography (gCBCT) imaging technique for lung cancer patients who undergo respiratory gating stereotactic
body radiation therapy (RG-SBRT). We propose a next-generation imaging paradigm, nonstop gated CBCT
(ngCBCT) to reduce imaging time, lower imaging dose, and preserve image quality, thereby improving patient
experience and treatment outcome. This innovation is also critical for expanding the adoption of respiratory
gating techniques in other tumor sites affected by respiratory motion, such as the pancreas and liver.

title: Lung Injury in ONcologic Stem cell transplants (LIONS)
text:
Pulmonary toxicity is a major driver of morbidity and mortality after pediatric hematopoietic cell transplantation
(HCT), but the mechanisms leading to lung injury are poorly understood. The Lung Injury in ONcologic Stem
cell transplants (LIONS) study will collect blood before and immediately after HCT in 400 patients, and assess
what molecular factors differ in patients who develop lung injury, versus those who do not. A better
understanding of what molecular changes lead to lung injury after HCT will permit the design of interventions to
limit this toxicity and thereby improve survival rates after HCT.

title: Bioinformatics and Molecular Mechanisms Core
text: PROJECT SUMMARY - BIOINFORMATICS AND MOLECULAR MECHANISMS CORE The Bioinformatics and Molecular Mechanisms Core (BMMC) is a central component of the Pennington- Louisiana NORC, supporting mechanistic research on nutrition, obesity, and metabolic health across the lifespan. Since its inception in 2005, the Core has provided turnkey access to advanced technologies in genomics and bioimaging, facilitating innovative research by lowering technical and analytical barriers— particularly for early-career investigators. In the current funding cycle, Core membership has grown to 109 individuals, reflecting a 65% increase in affiliated grant activity, now totaling $21.5 million in direct funding. To meet the rising demands of large-scale data generation and analysis, the NORC made a forward-looking decision to formally incorporate bioinformatics as a dedicated function within the Core. This strategic move is reflected in the renaming of the Core to the Bioinformatics and Molecular Mechanisms Core (BMMC), which now fully integrates Genomics, Bioimaging, and Bioinformatics services. This reorganization enhances the Core’s ability to deliver end-to-end support for complex experimental workflows—from initial consultation and study design through data analysis and publication. BMMC offers expert guidance on experimental design, technology selection, statistical analysis, and preparation of grant applications and manuscripts, ensuring that projects meet the highest standards of rigor, reproducibility, and transparency (Aim 1). The Core provides access to state-of-the-art equipment, technical expertise, and customized protocols for genomics and high- content imaging studies, along with hands-on support for pilot projects and tailored training for investigators and their staff (Aim 2). Bioinformatics capabilities encompass the processing and analysis of next-generation sequencing and imaging datasets, maintenance of analytical software, and assistance in leveraging public datasets relevant to investigator needs (Aim 3). These integrated services are continuously refined through regular assessments, adoption of emerging technologies, and increased interoperability across cores to better serve NORC investigators (Aim 4). Through its expert leadership, seamless technological infrastructure, and continued support especially for early-career scientists, the BMMC empowers NORC researchers to pursue cutting-edge, data-driven investigations that advance understanding of obesity and metabolic disease.

title: Mechanistic studies of the NRF2-Methylosome interaction in lung cancer.
text:
Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer deaths in the world, and while treatment options have improved,
there remains a tremendous need for targeted therapies to improve lung cancer survival rates. Our lab has
recently identified PRMT5 as a putative modulator of NRF2, an oncogenic transcription factor that is selectively
essential in lung cancers, which could serve as a more tractable target for the development of novel therapies.
This project will combine biochemical and functional genomic approaches to determine the molecular
mechanisms that link NRF2 and PRMT5 and assess its potential as a target for novel cancer targeted therapies.

title: Molecular analysis of ASH1L
text:
ASH1L is frequently amplified and mutated in human cancers. Upregulated enzymatic activity of
ASH1L is particularly associated with aggressive forms of leukemias. The proposed studies will
lead to a better understanding of how the ASH1L signaling pathways can be therapeutically
manipulated and may help to develop new strategies to prevent or treat cancer.

title: Arkansas Bioinformatics Consortium
text:
The FDA ability to protect the public health is directly related to its ability to access and utilize the latest
scientific data. Increased proficiency in collecting, presenting, validating, understanding, and drawing
quantitative inference from the massive volume of new scientific results is necessary for success in that
effort. The complexity involved requires continued development of new tools available and being
developed within the realm of information technology, and the workshops proposed here will address
this need.
Specific Aims
 • Thoroughly understand the resources in Arkansas available for furthering the capabilities in
 bioinformatics and its associated needs, e.g., access to high speed computing capability and use
 of computational tools.
• Develop a set of plans to harness and grow those capabilities, especially those that are relevant
 to the needs of NCTR and FDA.
• Stimulate interest and capability across Arkansas in bioinformatics to produce a larger cadre of
 expertise as these plans are implemented.
• Enlist NCTR’s help in directing the effort toward seeking local, national and international data
 that can be more effectively analyzed to produce results needed by FDA and others, e.g.,
 reviewing decades of genomic/treatment data on myeloma patients at the University of
 Arkansas for Medical Sciences.
• Develop ways in which the Arkansas capabilities can be combined into a coordinated, synergistic
 force larger than the sum of its parts.
• Encourage students and faculty in the development of new models and techniques to be used in
 bioinformatics and related fields.
• Improve inter-institutional communication, including developing standardized bioinformatics
 curricula and more universal course acceptance.

title: Sex Differences in Regulatory Interneurons of the Striatum
text:
We have identified sexual dimorphism in interneurons of the basal ganglia; we hypothesize that this may
contribute to the marked sex differences in prevalence and presentation that characterizes several
neuropsychiatric disorders in which the basal ganglia are implicated. Here we characterize sex effects on
interneuron morphology, connectivity, gene expression, and activity, and identify the developmental mechanisms
that lead to these effects. In parallel with this important scientific work, this career development award will
advance the training of the PI, Dr. Meghan Van Zandt, as she moves to establish an independent program
focused on sex differences in basal ganglia function and neuropsychiatric disease.

title: Cancer Immunotherapy: Basic Mechanisms Informing Clinical Applications & Combinations
text:
Cancer immunotherapy strategies are highly effective, yet benefit only a subset of patients, as most individuals
either fail to respond or do so transiently then develop resistance. This Keystone Symposia conference will focus
on the mechanistic basis of failure of immunotherapies, explore new approaches to activating the immune
system, and highlight promising technologies, including spatial imaging and AI, to better understand the tumor
microenvironment. Bringing together basic, translational and clinical researchers from various scientific settings
will provide insights for future clinical applications and optimal combination therapies to address cancer treatment
needs.

title: Dissecting the synaptic and molecular mechanisms of cell-type-specific memory computation in hippocampal CA3
text:
This project will employ cutting-edge in vivo imaging, photo-tagging, and genetic manipulation techniques,
combined with computational modeling, to uncover the synaptic and molecular mechanisms that support cell-
type-specific memory computation in hippocampal CA3. By defining how distinct afferent inputs and neuronal
subtypes contribute to learning-related plasticity and population coding, this work will establish a multiscale
framework for understanding learning and memory. These insights may guide future strategies to treat cognitive
dysfunction associated with aging and neurological disease.

title: Understanding ethno-racial differences in AT(N)-defined heterogeneity profiles
text: Neuroanatomical heterogeneity in Alzheimer disease (AD) has important implications for clinical outcomes as well as patient-specific treatments, however, little is known regarding AD biomarker topographical patterns in ethno-racial groups as well as the effects of socio-demographic factors on heterogeneity. The present study utilizes the National Institute on Aging (NIA) - Alzheimer Association Research Framework and the NIA’s Health Disparities Framework to characterize heterogeneity in AT(N) imaging markers, as well as the effects of socio-demographic factors on heterogeneity, in a community-based population. This line of work will aid in guiding precision medicine and in recruitment efforts in clinical trials while highlighting potential health disparities.

title: Rib Fixation for Prevention of Proximal Junctional Kyphosis (PJK) in Adult Spinal Deformity Surgery
text:
Proximal junctional kyphosis (PJK) is an important problem following adult spinal deformity surgery. It is
characterized as an abnormal forward bending of the spine in the spinal segments immediately above the
instrumented segments, and can result in progressive kyphotic deformity, neurologic deficit, chronic pain, and
loss of function. The proposed studies will explore a novel surgical technique that uses rib fixation for PJK
prophylaxis in adult spinal deformity surgery.

title: Exploring genomic and cellular determinants of gene therapy durability
text:
While gene therapy has made major strides in the treatment of a broad range of diseases, many mechanisms
that control long-term expression and phenotypic improvements remain unknown. This work aims to build an in-
depth analysis of the genetic and cellular determinants of gene therapy longevity which is consistent with the
goals of NIGMS.
